# AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models

Sidharth Sinha Affiliation: Microsoft, M365 Research, India    Anson
Bastos Affiliation: Microsoft, M365 Research, India Correspondence to:
<ansonbastos@microsoft.com>    Xuchao Zhang Affiliation: Microsoft, M365
Research, Redmond Correspondence to: <xuchaozhang@microsoft.com>   
Akshay Nambi Affiliation: Microsoft Research, India Correspondence to:
<Akshay.Nambi@microsoft.com>    Chetan Bansal Affiliation: Microsoft,
M365 Research, Redmond    Saravan Rajmohan Affiliation: Microsoft, M365
Research, Redmond

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) excel in open domains but struggle in
specialized settings with limited data and evolving knowledge. Existing
domain adaptation practices rely heavily on manual trial-and-error
processes, incur significant hyperparameter complexity, and are highly
sensitive to data and user preferences, all under the high cost of LLM
training. Moreover, the interactions and transferability of
hyperparameter choices across models/domains remain poorly understood,
making adaptation gains uncertain even with substantial effort. To solve
these challenges, we present _AutoAdapt_, a novel end-to-end automated
framework for efficient and reliable LLM domain adaptation. _AutoAdapt_
leverages curated knowledge bases from literature and open-source
resources to reduce expert intervention. To narrow the search space, we
design a novel multi-agent debating system in which proposal and critic
agents iteratively interact to align user intent and incorporate data
signals and best practices into the planning process. To optimize
hyperparameters under tight budgets, we propose _AutoRefine_, a novel
LLM-based surrogate that replaces costly black-box search. Across 10
tasks, _AutoAdapt_ achieves a 25% average relative accuracy improvement
over state-of-the-art Automated Machine Learning baselines with minimal
overhead.

###### Keywords: 

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced the state of the art
in natural language processing, enabling impressive performance across a
wide spectrum of tasks and domains. However, despite their broad
pre-training, LLMs often fall short when applied to specialized domains
where data is scarce, proprietary, or subject to privacy constraints.
Further, in scenarios where data evolves with time, pretrained LLMs
would not have the updated knowledge. In such settings, domain
adaptation of LLMs is imperative by resorting to techniques like
in-context prompting ([Dong et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)) using retrieval
from current data (RAG) ([Lewis et al., 2020](#bib.bib20)) or finetuning
the models (SFT) ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)) on new data for
optimal performance. The current process of adapting LLMs to a specific
task is largely manual and remains limited to a set of best practices,
assuming a one-template-fits-all approach across tasks and models.
Further, effective fine tuning relies on expert knowledge because small
choices in data, objectives, and training settings can strongly affect
the performance.

Domain adaptation for LLMs involves a series of intricate steps:
curating domain-specific datasets, selecting appropriate model
architectures, configuring prompting or fine-tuning strategies, and
iteratively optimizing hyperparameters for optimal performance. Each
decision point, ranging from model selection, context engineering,
training technique (e.g., supervised fine-tuning (SFT),
parameter-efficient adaptation (PeFT) e.g. LoRA/Prefix Tuning,
preference alignment e.g. DPO) to the choice of learning rates, batch
sizes, and regularization techniques, can significantly impact the final
model’s quality, stability and cost. The challenge of exploring the vast
search space is compounded in LLMs due to the high time and cost of
finetuning these large models. The combinatorial explosion of possible
configurations, coupled with the high time and resource utility, means
that even experienced teams must engage in extensive trial-and-error,
often spending weeks or months to achieve robust, high-quality results.

Recent research ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Trirat et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30); [Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib35); [Zhang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib36)) has explored automating general Machine Learning (ML)
pipelines using agent-based frameworks offering partial solutions for
model selection and hyperparameter tuning, albeit in the general ML
domain. However, the following challenges exist: 1) Existing methods
either rely on the pretraining knowledge or in-context learning ability
of LLMs, which we show is insufficient for the task of LLM adaptation.
Further, retrieval based methods ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib13);
[Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) lack a structured knowledge base of
LLM use cases, limiting their usage to only classical ML methods. 2)
These approaches typically rely on exhaustive or heuristic search
strategies, which are computationally expensive and ill-suited to the
scale and complexity of LLM adaptation. 3) Existing methods rely on the
LLM agents to generate code. However, agents may have limited and
outdated pretraining context on LLM adaptation. This results in low
success rate for end-to-end runs as we show in our experiments. 4) LLM
adaptation pipelines often require multiple stages such as pretraining,
followed by finetuning, alignment, in-context prompting using RAG
techniques and so on. Existing methods fail in planning such a
multi-stage pipeline due to a lack of a structured and well defined
hierarchical plan. 5) LLMs incur an exorbitant cost and latency for
training and thus standard Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) techniques
employed in existing methods ([Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) will
hardly scale to LLM adaptation. 6) Most agents do not consider the data
characteristics and explicit adherence to user preferences during the
planning stage or merely loop on failing execution which degrades
efficiency.

To address these challenges, we introduce _AutoAdapt_, an automated
domain adaptation framework that proposes to solve the adaptation
problem as a multi-agent system grounded in a knowledge-driven
hierarchical workflow. We further use Gaussian processes ([Beckers,
2021](#bib.bib3)) for probabilistic function estimation, modeling
uncertainty over the adaptation objective function. Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
shows the user flow of _AutoAdapt_, where the user inputs the task,
data, and constraints and the system outputs the domain adapted LLM.

![Refer to caption](2603.08181v1/autoadapt_concept_figure.png)

Figure 1: _AutoAdapt_ takes as input the user instruction and dataset
and delivers the domain adapted LLM based on user constraint

_AutoAdapt_ leverages a structured directed acyclic graph, called
“Adaptation Configuration Graph” (ACG), that incorporates the LLM
adaptation workflow knowledge. This graph contains hierarchical decision
nodes (e.g. RAG vs SFT, SFT using LoRA or Prefix Tuning etc.) and
parameter nodes (e.g. learning rate, epochs, batch size to explore for
SFT). The framework is composed of a system of proposal and critic
agents to generate, debate, verify and refine executable pipelines. We
ground the multi-agent system by integrating best practices from
thousands of open-source models and datasets, as well as user-specified
requirements and data characteristics. We further perform online
retrieval from web sources and literature. Thus, _AutoAdapt_
dramatically reduces the need for manual intervention and expert
oversight. This produces an adaptation pipeline with narrowed search
spaces (e.g. $`1e^{-4}\leq\texttt{learning rate}\leq 1e^{-6}`$) to
optimize. The framework further incorporates a feedback-driven
optimization loop, called _AutoRefine_, to optimize parameters (e.g.
exact SFT parameters like $`\texttt{learning rate}=2e^{-5}`$ from the
narrowed search space). AutoRefine efficiently explores the
hyperparameter space using LLM-based oracle that factors performance
from prior runs. However naive usage of LLMs to predict performance
(surrogate modeling) ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)) in the
multi-dimensional LLM hyperparameter space, is prone to hallucination.
We propose to solve this by grounding the LLM surrogate with function
estimation techniques.

Through extensive empirical evaluation across diverse domains, including
mathematical and general reasoning, medical question answering, legal
analysis, programming, agent tool calling, e-commerce, and real world
cloud incident diagnosis, we demonstrate that _AutoAdapt_ consistently
outperforms existing AutoML baselines, delivering significant accuracy
gains with minimal additional computational overhead (w.r.t. default
choices). By _automating the end-to-end LLM adaptation process_,
_AutoAdapt_ makes robust, domain-specific LLMs accessible to a broader
range of users and organizations, _bridging the gap between cutting-edge
research and practical real-world applications_. In summary:

- •
  We propose a novel method for end-to-end LLM domain adaptation guided
  by a structured adaptation workflow ensuring a high success rate in
  executing the pipeline. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first
  to propose an automated domain adaptation framework for LLMs.
- •
  We curate a knowledge base for LLM domain adaptation from open source
  implementations, datasets, models, and best practices to ground the
  recommendations.
- •
  We address the exponential search space in LLM adaptation, by
  designing a novel multi-agent framework that traverses the adaptation
  graph incorporating the user constraints, data signals, and best
  practices, to recommend adaptation pipelines and hyperparameter
  ranges.
- •
  We formulate a first-of-its-kind probabilistic function estimation
  based technique in conjunction with LLMs to efficiently perform
  refinement of the parameter choices and ranges for the selected
  pipeline.
- •
  We conduct extensive experiments on datasets spanning various
  benchmark and real world datasets across multiple domains to
  demonstrate the efficacy of our method in adapting LLMs to the
  specialized tasks.

There exists a plethora of works in literature on automated machine
learning. Here, we focus on agentic solutions to automate this process.
In agentic literature, prior works such as ([Zhang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib36); [Shen et al., 2023](#bib.bib27); [Hong et al.,
2024](#bib.bib16); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)) focus on specific
aspects of the ML training pipeline such as data preparation, analysis
or HPO etc. MLCopilot ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)) was one of the
first agentic systems tackling general ML pipelines, using an offline
stage to build knowledge from experience and an online retrieval stage.
Similarly DS-Agent ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)) proposes to use LLM
agents along with case based reasoning (CBR) to come up with generic
data science pipelines for a task. AutoML-Agent ([Trirat et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30)) employs a multi-agent LLM framework using retrieved
knowledge bases to automate generic ML training pipelines. These methods
are not tailored to LLMs and fall short in reliably planning and
executing complex, multi-stage LLM adaptation workflows. Unlike prior
methods that typically support only single-stage training pipelines,
_AutoAdapt_ provides a comprehensive framework for full domain
adaptation pipelines, including multi-stage processes such as in-context
prompting (e.g. RAG), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), alignment (DPO) and
so on. _AutoAdapt_ aims to _reliably_ and _efficiently_ generate
user-aligned executable _LLM adaptation_ plans, overcoming the
limitations of existing AutoML systems. Please refer the Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Related Works ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
for further details.

## 3 Problem Formulation

We formulate domain adaptation of large language models (LLMs) as a
multi–stage optimization problem. Let $`D=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$
denote the user–provided dataset for a downstream task, and let $`c`$
represent the user context (e.g., hardware constraints, latency
requirements, or user preferences such as PEFT vs. full fine–tuning). An
adapted model is constructed through a sequence of $`T`$ transformation
stages (e.g., continual pretraining, supervised fine–tuning, preference
optimization, inference–time augmentation). Each stage $`t`$ is
parameterized by a configuration $`h_{t}\in\mathcal{H}_{t}`$. The final
model produced by the pipeline is denoted as
$`f_{\theta}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{T}).`$ _AutoAdapt_ _differs from existing
AutoML techniques in this aspect of planning each component of the
pipeline sequentially following the hierarchy of the adaptation graph._
Our goal is to find a feasible configuration sequence
$`(h_{1},\ldots,h_{T})`$ that minimizes expected task loss:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\min_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{T}\in\mathcal{H}(c)}\;\;\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim D}\left[L\big(f_{\theta}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{T})(x),y\big)\right],
``` |  |

where the feasible set $`\mathcal{H}(c)`$ encodes context‑dependent
constraints such as GPU memory, training budget, or user‑specified
preferences.

Prior‑Guided Sequential Configuration Space: Each stage $`t`$ has a set
of hyperparameters, $`h_{t}=\{h_{t,1},\ldots,h_{t,n_{t}}\},`$ and rather
than selecting all hyperparameters jointly, we construct them
sequentially. Let $`h_{<t}=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{t-1})`$ denote
configurations from previous stages, and
$`h_{t,<i}=(h_{t,1},\ldots,h_{t,i-1})`$ denote earlier choices within
stage $`t`$. Define a prior‑guided feasible region for stage $`t`$ as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{P}_{t}(c,h_{<t})=\left\{h_{t}:h_{t,i}\in\mathcal{P}_{t,i}(c,h_{<t},h_{t,<i}),\;i=1,\ldots,n_{t}\right\},
``` |  |

where each sub‑policy $`\mathcal{P}_{t,i}`$ incorporates domain
knowledge (e.g., best‑practice hyperparameter ranges), conditional
dependencies (e.g., selecting LoRA activates
$`\text{rank},\alpha,\text{dropout}`$), and context constraints. The
multi–stage adaptation problem thus becomes:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\min_{h_{1},\ldots,h_{T}}\;\;`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim D}\left[L\big(f_{\theta}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{T})(x),y\big)\right]\quad`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad h_{t}\in\mathcal{P}_{t}(c,h_{<t}),\;\forall t`$ |  |

###### Proposition 3.1.

Let $`\mathcal{H}(c)`$ be the feasible configuration space and
$`\mathcal{P}(c)=\mathcal{P}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{P}_{T}`$ the
prior‑guided subspace. Denote the expected task loss as
$`L_{\mathbb{E}}(h)`$, the optimal loss over the full space is
$`L_{\mathcal{H}}^{*}=\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}(c)}L_{\mathbb{E}}(h)`$ and
the optimal loss over the prior‑guided space is
$`L_{\mathcal{P}}^{*}=\min_{h\in\mathcal{P}(c)}L_{\mathbb{E}}(h)`$.
Considering $`L_{\mathbb{E}}(h)`$ is Lipschitz continuous in
hyperparameters, the prior‑guided subspace satisfies the generalized
$`\varepsilon`$-covering bound:

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       L_{\mathcal{P}}^{*}\;\leq\;L_{\mathcal{H}}^{*}\;+\;L\varepsilon,
       ```                                                               |     |

where $`L`$ is the Lipschitz constant and $`\varepsilon`$ is the
distance between the optimal parameters in $`\mathcal{H}(c)`$ and
$`\mathcal{P}(c)`$.

The above result is straightforward to verify after continuous
relaxation ([Boyd & Vandenberghe, 2004](#bib.bib4)) of the discrete
space. It implies that restricting search to the prior‑guided subspace
incurs at most a controlled additive suboptimality while yielding
dramatically improved tractability. For the optimization over the
constrained search space we propose to use LLMs together with function
estimation (using Gaussian process) techniques. More details on Gaussian
processes can be found in Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Preliminaries ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
and [Beckers 2021](#bib.bib3).

Note, the above formulation is intended solely for clarity of exposition
and the proposed method does not depend on the stated assumptions.

## 4 Method

![Refer to caption](2603.08181v1/autoadapt_overview_detail.png)

Figure 2: Framework Overview: *AutoAdapt* processes user data and task
definitions, integrates best practices, generates an executable training
pipeline, and refines an intermediate model to produce a deliverable
model for users.

This section details the components of our method. Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4 Method ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
gives an overview of *AutoAdapt*. The user provides the task
description, data and constraints. *AutoAdapt* then runs to find the
optimal adaptation pipeline through the following workflow: (i) The
Adaptation Configuration Graph (ACG) is executed to decompose the
decision making in a structured workflow. (ii) A multi‑agent debate
pipeline is run at every node of the ACG to propose an executable
adaptation plan with narrowed hyperparameter ranges. The multi-agent
system is grounded in best practices from literature (processed in a KB
or queried real time from web search, huggingface, github etc.) (iii) On
obtaining the adaptation pipeline from the multi-agent system,
AutoRefine is run to obtain the exact parameter set. AutoRefine is a
feedback‑driven optimization loop that combines LLM surrogate reasoning
with probabilistic function estimation to efficiently and effectively
select hyperparameters. (iv) Once the optimization is complete, the
pipeline is executed to produce the adapted LLM for the user task.

### 4.1 Best Practices Knowledge Base

The multi-agentic system needs to be grounded in the real world LLM
usage ecosystem. For this we curate the best-pratices corpus from public
LLM ecosystems capturing model choices, training pipelines, and
hyperparameters at scale. The sources include Hugging Face model/data
cards and tags (e.g., sft, dpo, domain tags like medical), PwC
leaderboards and notebooks (github, unsloth) and practitioner guides on
web. This corpus helps in the hierarchical decision of strategy
selection (e.g., RAG vs SFT, LoRA vs. Prefix Tuning), model choice (e.g.
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct vs Qwen2.5-3B) and hyperparameter ranges (e.g.,
learning_rate, batch_size etc.).

We extract knowledge from $`\sim 100`$ K model and data cards available
from the sources. We prompt an LLM to extract features such as model
family, size, training pipeline and parameters if available. Similarly
for the datasets we extract the dataset size, domain, best performing
models among other details. These structured extractions (training
technique, dataset size, hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, source
links) form the schema of the KB.

Extraction pipeline The system applies prompt‑driven parsers over
model/data cards and notebooks to obtain details like training
technique, model/dataset size, hyperparameters, evaluation, model source
etc. The entries are indexed in a vector store by task description,
domain and dataset descriptors. The KB is then queried given an incoming
task (e.g. medical QA), returning top‑k matched datasets/models and
their reported training configurations to initialize the planning.
Please refer $`\lx@sectionsign`$
[G](#A7 "Appendix G Best-Practices Knowledge Base ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
for details.

### 4.2 Adaptation Configuration Graph (ACG)

![Refer to caption](2603.08181v1/figures/autoadapt_acg.png)

Figure 3: Hierarchical Configuration Determination Using a Domain
Adaptation Configuration Graph (ACG)

The ACG formalizes adaptation planning as a directed acyclic graph. The
nodes are of two types: selection nodes for discrete strategy/technique
(e.g. RAG vs SFT) choices and parameter nodes for hyperparameters within
the selected technique (e.g. learning_rate in SFT).

Construction: We construct the ACG manually based on best practices. The
start selection node selects between RAG, SFT and Alignment . Along SFT,
the decision path includes PEFT and within PEFT the choices include
`{LoRA, DoRA, Prefix Tuning}`. The selection nodes for Alignment can be
invoked post SFT or without SFT (using a pretrained model). The choices
inside Alignment include `{DPO, RLHF}`. The Parameter nodes, present at
the leaf of a traversed path, represent the decision for the
continuous/categorical parameter ranges for e.g. parameters for SFT
include epochs, learning_rate, LoRA rank/alpha/dropout, batch_size,
gradient_accumulation, quantization etc. Edges encode dependencies e.g.
choosing LoRA in PEFT selection node activates the dependent Parameter
node to decide the search space for
`{lora_r, lora_alpha, lora_dropout}`.

Hierarchical Decision over the ACG: Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Adaptation Configuration Graph (ACG) ‣ 4 Method ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
shows a sample ACG workflow. The planner (multi-agent debate system
outlined next) starts at high‑level decision nodes (e.g., RAG, SFT and
Alignment) and traverses until leaf nodes (complete executable plan). At
each node, the planner retrieves information from the best‑practice KB
and aggregates them with user constraints (compute/time/budget) to
decide the pipeline. This structured approach constrains search making
the adaptation efficient and ensures reliable execution. The traversed
path need not adhere to a linear chain graph but could also involve
multiple paths e.g. SFT followed by Alignment or RAG as decided by the
system.

### 4.3 Multi-Agent Debate Planner

In order to make the decision at the nodes of the ACG, we design a
multi-agent pipeline. The selection nodes of the ACG could also be
treated as hyperparameters and evaluated. However this increases the
search space which becomes infeasible for the case of LLMs. Thus we need
an efficient planning system akin to expert humans selecting techniques
from knowledge or literature.

The multi‑agent system consists of proposal and critic agents that
debate in turns to come up with the final decision on the technique,
model and parameter ranges. Below we briefly describe the agents (with
details in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Multi Agent System ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models"))

Proposal Agents: Proposal agents are responsible for constructing and
iteratively refining candidate domain adaptation pipelines. These agents
are (i) *best practice agent*: consolidates empirical knowledge from
prior training pipelines, model cards, and published benchmarks, and
(ii) *knowledge retrieval agent*: dynamically retrieves evidence from
recent literature, technical reports, and online resources. (iii)
*research agent*: utilizes the research information retrieved from
arxiv, KBs etc. to propose techniques. These agents initialize the
search process in regions of the configuration space that historically
yield strong performance while remaining responsive to emerging
techniques.

Critic Agents: Critic agents verify the proposed configurations against
user, data and resource constraints. (i) The *user agent* enforces
user‑specified requirements, such as compute budgets, training
preferences, methodological restrictions, and domain‑specific
constraints. In parallel, (ii) the *data agent* performs data‑centric
critique by analyzing statistics of the target dataset, including scale,
token distributions, domain characteristics etc., and mapping these
signals to concrete constraints on adaptation choices.

After each round of debate, an *aggregator agent* aggregates the
proposals and critiques. The proposal agents further revise the
proposals based on the critiques and unsatisfied constraints. In this
manner, each ACG node undergoes *proposal $`\xrightarrow{}`$ critique
$`\xrightarrow{}`$ revision* iterations. The loop terminates when all
active constraints are satisfied and the plan is deemed executable (with
runnable code). The AutoRefine module is then invoked to decide the
exact parameter values.

### 4.4 AutoRefine

This module decides the optimal hyperparameter set using an LLM
surrogate method. Prior works ([Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)) have
shown that transformers (and thus LLMs) have limitations in time series
forecasting. This issue is bound to be amplified in the multivariate
forecasting by works using LLMs as surrogates ([Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib24)) to predict results. Thus we propose a principled
approach grounded in function estimation theory to guide the surrogate
modeling from prior knowledge of historic runs. We use Gaussian Process
(GP) model for function estimation.

Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.4 AutoRefine ‣ 4 Method ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
provides a pseudo-code for AutoRefine. We start by sampling a coreset
([Jubran et al., 2019](#bib.bib19)) of the data for efficient execution.
We then perform few ($`\sim 3`$) execution runs on the selected pipeline
(e.g. SFT) by invoking an LLM to sample initial parameters from the
narrowed search space (lines 2-5). Inspired by ([Requeima et al.,
2024](#bib.bib25)), we prompt the LLM to predict the results along each
parameter dimension from the evaluated points (lines 9-12). We reason
that predicting the trend along each parameter axis will help reduce
hallucinations compared to directly estimating the results on the higher
dimensional space. These historic and predicted results are used to
train a GP model to obtain a function estimation of the remaining points
in the search space (line 13). Note the GP model requires hundreds of
data points to learn the function and it is not possible to
finetune/evaluate LLMs for many iterations. Hence, we obtain the
parameter-axis wise trends of the results to augment data. Once the
model of the results over the search space is obtained we need an
acquisition function that would maximize the result of the acquired
hyperparameter set. For acquisition, we find the optimal point of
function using LBFGS ([Liu & Nocedal, 1989](#bib.bib21)) (after
continuous relaxation of the categorical variables), starting from each
of the historic evaluated samples (lines 14-18). Post discretization,
the LLM is prompted in-context with these optimal points to choose the
next parameter set to evaluate on (lines 19-21), balancing exploration
and exploitation. Thus the LLM surrogate is guided by the optimal
hyperparameter as per the estimated function that is grounded in results
from prior runs, reducing hallucinations. We allow a maximum of
$`\mathcal{B}`$ (loops starting line 2,7) function evaluations (e.g.
finetuning followed by testing on validation set) on the selected
parameters. Following theoretical result analyzes the regret (difference
of result on selected parameter from true optimal) bounds of AutoRefine
(cf. Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
for details). The regret grows sub-linearly with the iterations and the
constants are improved by the LLM augmentation factor.

###### Lemma 4.1.

Pick $`\delta\in(0,1)`$. Then with probability at least $`1-\delta`$,
the cumulative regret of the algorithm in
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.4 AutoRefine ‣ 4 Method ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
is bounded as
$`R_{T_{a}}=\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{T}{F_{a}}log^{2}\left(\frac{T}{F_{a}}\right)}\right)`$.
Further, to guarantee the average regret $`r_{T}\leq\varepsilon`$ for
some $`\varepsilon>0`$, we have
$`T_{a}=\Omega\!\Bigg(\frac{\ln^{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{F_{a}\varepsilon^{2}}\Bigg)`$.
Here $`T_{a},T`$ is the number of actual function evaluations and total
iterations (actual evals + LLM predictions) of the algorithm
respectively, $`F_{a}`$ is the LLM surrogate augmentation factor

0:  Pipeline $`\mathcal{P}`$, Parameter space $`\Theta`$, Coreset
$`C\subseteq\texttt{Data}`$, LLM $`\mathcal{L}`$, GP kernel $`\kappa`$
(RBF), Budget $`\mathcal{B}`$, Augmentation Factor $`F_{a}`$

0:  Best configuration $`\theta^{\star}\in\Theta`$

1:  $`\mathcal{M}=\varnothing`$

2:  for $`k`$ in $`\mathcal{K}`$ do $`\triangleright`$ Warm start with
$`\mathcal{K}<\mathcal{B}`$ runs

3:   $`\theta^{(k)}\leftarrow\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{P})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Sample from parameter space

4:   $`\hat{y}^{k}\leftarrow\mathrm{Eval}(\mathcal{P},C,\theta^{(k)})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Evaluate pipeline and observe outcomes

5:   $`\mathcal{M}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}\cup(\theta^{k},\hat{y}^{k})`$

6:  end for

7:  while $`!\texttt{Converged}`$ or $`\texttt{niters}=\mathcal{B-K}`$
do

8:   $`\mathcal{M_{L}}\leftarrow M`$

9:   for $`j`$ in $`\texttt{dim}(\theta)`$ do $`\triangleright`$
Univariate LLM forecasting along each parameter, keeping others fixed

10:
   $`\{(\theta_{j}^{(s)},\tilde{y}_{j}^{(s)})\}\leftarrow\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{P},\texttt{parameter=j},\texttt{s=}\lceil\frac{F_{a}}{\texttt{dim}(\theta)}\rceil)`$

11:
   $`\mathcal{M_{L}}\leftarrow\mathcal{M_{L}}\cup\{(\theta_{j}^{(s)},\tilde{y}_{j}^{(s)})\}`$

12:   end for

13:
  $`\mathcal{S}(\theta),\mu(\theta),\sigma(\theta)\leftarrow\mathrm{GP}(\mathcal{M_{L}},\kappa)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Fit GP surrogate and obtain UCB score, mean,
uncertainty over $`\Theta`$

14:   $`M_{\texttt{opt}}\leftarrow\varnothing`$

15:   for $`t\in|\mathcal{M}|`$ do $`\triangleright`$ Optimize the
estimated density from each evaluated point

16:
   $`(\theta^{t}_{\texttt{opt}},y^{t})\leftarrow\texttt{LBFGS}(S(\theta),\theta^{t})`$

17:
   $`M_{\texttt{opt}}\leftarrow M_{\texttt{opt}}\cup(\theta^{t}_{\texttt{opt}},y^{t})`$

18:   end for

19:
  $`\theta_{s}\leftarrow\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M,P,M_{\texttt{opt}}},\theta)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Acquisition function to sample new set of parameters
for evaluation

20:   Evaluate
$`\hat{y}_{s}\leftarrow\mathrm{Eval}(\mathcal{P},C,\theta_{s})`$

21:
  $`\mathcal{M}\leftarrow\mathcal{M}\cup\{(\theta_{s},\hat{y}_{s})\}`$

22:  end while

23:  return
$`\theta^{\star}\leftarrow\arg\max_{(\theta,y)\in\mathcal{M}}y`$

Algorithm 1 Overall Procedure of AutoRefine

## 5 Experiments

![Refer to caption](2603.08181v1/figures/radar_three_panels.png)

Figure 4: Success Rate (SR), Normalized Performance Score (NPS),
Cumulative Score (CS) comparing *AutoAdapt* with baseline methods across
datasets. Higher score indicates better results. *AutoAdapt* outperforms
SoTA baselines across datasets. Detailed results are in
$`\lx@sectionsign`$
[I](#A9 "Appendix I Detailed Results ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models").

We design our experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of *AutoAdapt*
and aim to answer the following research questions (RQ): RQ1: Can
*AutoAdapt* effectively recommend adaptation pipelines across real world
and benchmark datasets? RQ2: What is the importance of each component of
*AutoAdapt*? RQ3: How do the results converge on scaling the iterations?
RQ4: What is the effectiveness of AutoRefine module compared to Bayesian
Optimization? RQ5: How efficient is *AutoAdapt*?

Datasets We conduct experiments on the following benchmark datasets
(details in $`\lx@sectionsign`$
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Datasets ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")):
MATH ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib14)), MedQA ([Jin et al.,
2020](#bib.bib18)), CaseHold ([Zheng et al., 2021](#bib.bib37)), ARC
([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib6)), MBPP+ ([Liu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib22)), Ecomm ([Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)), Entail
([Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)), When2Call ([Ross et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26)). In order to test the adaptation to real world
setting, we also evaluate on proprietary datasets containing
pre-engineering level math questions (PEM) and root cause analysis of
cloud incidents (RCA).

Metrics: We report the accuracy for task-specific benchmarks and compute
overhead in GPU hours and estimated cost (\$ value). Additionally, we
study convergence stability and the number of iterations to reach
optimal configurations.

Evaluation Protocol: *AutoAdapt* was run with its full pipeline: ACG
based hierarchical decision making, Best practice KB, multi-agent debate
planner, and AutoRefine. Baselines were executed using their recommended
workflows and default hyperparameter tuning strategies. Where baselines
fail to directly produce executable pipelines, we perform minimal
corrective edits to ensure executability for each error, run and repeat
till success. We report success rate (SR) as the reciprocal of the count
of these iterations. All experiments were repeated three times to ensure
consistency and the average is reported. Baselines: We compare
*AutoAdapt* against the following SoTA Agentic approaches: 1) MLCopilot
([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)): 2) DS-Agent ([Guo et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib13), ICML’24) 3) AutoMLAgent ([Trirat et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib30), ICML’25)

Implementation Details We implement *AutoAdapt* as an end-to-end
pipeline integrated with the Hugging Face model hub. Due to resource
constraints, we perform adaptation on models less than 15B parameters
from the following family: Qwen, Llama, Phi, Mistral. All runs were
executed on a single 4x A100 GPU with mixed precision enabled (bf16) to
ensure reproducibility and resource efficiency. In AutoRefine, the
Gaussian process (GP) model for function estimation was trained using
the GPyTorch framework ([Gardner et al., 2021](#bib.bib10)) for maximum
of 50 iterations to avoid overfitting and to enhance efficiency.
Inspired by ([Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)), we report success rate
(SR), Normalized Performance score (NPS) and a Comprehensive score (CS)
averaging SR and NPS, for methods over k(=3) runs. NPS is the
task-specific accuracy for our datasets. To select a coreset (by default
10%) of the data for finetuning/evaluation in AutoRefine we make use of
([Guo et al., 2022](#bib.bib12)). Note finetuning/evaluation using the
final pipeline is done on the entire train/test set. All baselines and
*AutoAdapt* were constrained by identical underlying LLM (GPT-4.1-mini),
resource budgets and evaluated under the same conditions to ensure
fairness.

## 6 Results

Main Results (RQ1) Figure
[4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
shows the SR, NPS and CPS metrics in the *template-free* (TF) setting
where methods are allowed to choose any technique, model etc. for
solving the task. We report the average scores from 3 independent runs
for all evaluation metrics. *AutoAdapt* consistently achieves the
highest performance across nearly all datasets and metrics. Table
[2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6 Results ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
shows the *template-aware* (TA) results with the model, technique (SFT)
and epochs fixed to ensure comparison across methods for hyperparameter
selection. We observe that *AutoAdapt* outperforms the generic AutoML
methods by a large margin. These results demonstrate that *AutoAdapt*’s
structured planning, prior‑guided configuration, and iterative
refinement enable more reliable and consistently superior domain
adaptation compared to existing automated baselines, making it effective
for LLM adaptation to downstream tasks. Further we show the results of
*AutoAdapt* with the constraints of choosing RAG and alignment (DPO)
pipelines on the PEM dataset. We see from figure
[6(a)](#S6.F6.sf1 "Figure 6(a) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ 6 Results ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
that compared to the baseline of human tuned or HF defaults our method
performs significantly better, indicating *AutoAdapt*’s effectiveness in
optimizing the LLM adaptation pipeline irrespective of underlying
technique.

Ablation Study (RQ2) Figure
[5(a)](#S6.F5.sf1 "Figure 5(a) ‣ Figure 5 ‣ 6 Results ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
summarizes the incremental impact of AutoAdapt’s principal components on
task accuracy, on the MedQA dataset. Specifically, we start with the
base LLM, then add the ACG planning, best practices, multi-agent
pipeline, AutoRefine (w/o and with GP). We note that on addition of
every component, the results improve indicating the importance of the
modules.

Hyperparameter Study (RQ3) Figure
[5(b)](#S6.F5.sf2 "Figure 5(b) ‣ Figure 5 ‣ 6 Results ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
examines the sensitivity of AutoAdapt to two parameters, namely number
of AutoRefine trials and multi‑agent debate rounds, on the MedQA
dataset. We observe a sharp gain for AutoRefine when increasing trials
from 1 to 2, followed by further increase at 5 trials and then a plateau
This indicates the effectiveness of autorefine in efficiently converging
to the optimal set of parameters in few trials. In parallel, multi‑agent
rounds show steady, monotonic improvements suggesting that additional
proposal–critique cycles systematically reduce planning bias and improve
configuration quality. This is suggestive that a modest budget of 5-10
AutoRefine trials and 2 debate rounds is sufficient to yield optimal
results.

Effectiveness of AutoRefine (RQ4) Figure
[6(b)](#S6.F6.sf2 "Figure 6(b) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ 6 Results ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
compares AutoRefine with a standard Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO)
baseline across increasing coreset fractions (0.01→1.0), reporting both
accuracy and wall‑clock time. HPO was performed using the Optuna
framework ([Akiba et al., 2019](#bib.bib1)) with auto_sampler, till
desired accuracy was achieved or maximum budget was attained. AutoRefine
consistently achieves higher or comparable accuracy at all fractions,
with a stable performance while being efficient. In practice, these
results support using small coresets with AutoRefine to capture most of
the achievable accuracy at a fraction of the cost of standard HPO.

Time and Cost Analysis (RQ5) Figure
[7](#S6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 6 Results ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
quantifies the monetary and time cost incurred by AutoAdapt. In panel
(a), the stacked breakdown shows the most fraction of time and LLM cost
of the system are concentrated in the AutoRefine phase. The reasoning is
that AutoRefine runs over multiple iterations as compared to planning in
order to find the optimal configuration. Panels (b) and (c) report the
time and monetary overheads at the task level. Averaged across datasets,
*AutoAdapt*’s performance gains ($`>7\%`$) outpace its incremental
time/cost ($`\sim`$ 15 mins / \$4), confirming a favorable trade-off,
validating the system’s efficacy for real‑world LLM domain adaptation.

## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce *AutoAdapt*, an automated framework for
domain adaptation of large language models. *AutoAdapt* ensures reliable
planning using a structured workflow graph. The proposed multi-agent
pipeline grounded in best practices KB narrows the search space.
Further, AutoRefine performs efficient optimization of the pipeline
hyperparameters using a novel LLM guided algorithm grounded in
probabilistic function estimation. Through extensive experiments across
diverse domains, we show that *AutoAdapt* consistently outperforms SoTA
AutoML baselines. *AutoAdapt* takes the first step towards end to end
automation of LLM adaptation to real world scenarios.

## Impact Statement

*AutoAdapt* aims to lower the technical and resource barriers to domain
adaptation of large language models by automating pipeline design,
configuration selection, and refinement. By enabling efficient
customization using smaller datasets and constrained budgets,
*AutoAdapt* can reduce redundant experimentation, lower computational
cost, and democratize access to high‑quality domain‑specific models for
researchers and practitioners with limited resources. This can benefit
applications in areas such as healthcare, education, legal analysis, and
scientific research, where domain expertise exists but large‑scale
machine learning infrastructure may not.

At the same time, *AutoAdapt* inherits the risks associated with
adapting LLMs to sensitive domains, including the potential
amplification of dataset biases or inappropriate behaviors if
user‑provided data is flawed or unrepresentative. While *AutoAdapt* does
not generate new data on its own in current state, its automation could
accelerate deployment of domain‑adapted models without sufficient human
review. To mitigate these risks, *AutoAdapt* is explicitly designed to
surface configuration decisions, maintain modularity across stages, and
enable human oversight through interpretable planning stages. We view
*AutoAdapt* as a decision‑support system rather than a replacement for
responsible model building evaluation.

Overall, *AutoAdapt* contributes to more efficient and transparent LLM
adaptation workflows, with the potential to reduce environmental impact
through compute savings while emphasizing the importance of careful
downstream evaluation and governance in real‑world deployments.
````
