````math
## Appendix A Preliminaries

Multi-agent frameworks have emerged as a powerful paradigm for complex
decision-making tasks, enabling distributed reasoning through
specialized agents that collaborate via a plethora of communication
workflows. In the context of automated machine learning and domain
adaptation, these frameworks allow decomposition of pipeline design into
modular decisions, improving scalability and adaptability compared to
monolithic approaches.

### A.1 Bayesian Optimisation

Bayesian optimization (BO) ([Frazier, 2018](#bib.bib9)) is a sequential
model-based approach for optimizing expensive black-box functions. It
assumes an unknown objective function $`f(\mathbf{x})`$ and models it
using a probabilistic surrogate, typically a Gaussian Process (GP)
([Beckers, 2021](#bib.bib3)). The GP defines a prior over functions and
updates it with observed data
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{t}`$. The posterior
predictive distribution at a new point $`\mathbf{x}_{*}`$ is:

|     |                                                                 |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mu(\mathbf{x}_{*})=k(\mathbf{x}_{*},X)^{\top}K^{-1}\mathbf{y},
       ```                                                              |     |

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sigma^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{*})=k(\mathbf{x}_{*},\mathbf{x}_{*})-k(\mathbf{x}_{*},X)^{\top}K^{-1}k(X,\mathbf{x}_{*})
``` |  |

where $`K`$ is the kernel matrix with entries
$`k(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j})`$.

The next query point is chosen by maximizing an acquisition function
$`\alpha(\mathbf{x})`$, which balances exploration and exploitation.
Common choices include: 1) Expected Improvement (EI):
$`\alpha_{\text{EI}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[\max(0,f(\mathbf{x})-f^{+})]=(\mu(\mathbf{x})-f^{+})\Phi(z)+\sigma(\mathbf{x})\phi(z)`$
where $`z=\frac{\mu(\mathbf{x})-f^{+}}{\sigma(\mathbf{x})}`$, $`f^{+}`$
is the best observed value, and $`\Phi,\phi`$ are the CDF and PDF of the
standard normal distribution. 2) Upper Confidence Bound (UCB):
$`\alpha_{\text{UCB}}(\mathbf{x})=\mu(\mathbf{x})+\kappa\sigma(\mathbf{x})`$
where $`\kappa>0`$ controls the exploration–exploitation trade-off.

## Appendix B Related Works

Recent advances in LLM-powered AutoML frameworks can be broadly
categorized into *static* and *dynamic* systems. Static recommendation
approaches, such as AutoMMLab ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)) , select
from a set of pre-prepared models and produce executable plans with
limited adaptability to user-specific requirements. Dynamic systems,
such as MLCopilot ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)), DS-Agent ([Guo
et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)) and AutoML-Agent ([Trirat et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30)), generate training plans and code , offering better
alignment with user tasks but often struggling with reliability and the
complexity for long, multi-stage adaptation pipelines.

Existing AutoML agents: AutoGPT ([Zhang et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)) and
HuggingGPT ([Shen et al., 2023](#bib.bib27)) connect LLMs with external
tools and models to solve generic AI tasks. Agents such as ([Guo et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13); [Hong et al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23)) focus on specific aspects of the ML training pipeline
such as data preparation, analysis or HPO and do not consider the end to
end pipeline for LLM adaptation. MLCopilot ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35)) uses a two-stage process: an offline stage to build a
knowledge pool from historical data and experience, and an online stage
to retrieve demonstrations and generate solutions based on new task
descriptions. DS-Agent proposes to use LLM agents along with case based
reasoning (CBR) to come up with generic data science pipelines for a
task. AutoML-Agent ([Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) is the closest
work related to our method. It employs a multi-agent LLM framework using
retrieved knowledge bases to automate generic ML training pipelines.
However, the method is not tailored to adaptation of LLMs which may not
require finetuning (RAG, prompt optimization etc.) or go beyond
finetuning (multi-stage RLHF, instruction tuning etc.). These methods
fall short in reliably planning and executing complex, multi-stage LLM
adaptation workflows.

Different from the above works, AutoAdapt introduces a hybrid
recommendation approach that combines the reliability of static planning
(using ACG) with the adaptability of dynamic systems (multi-agent system
guided by best practices KB). Unlike prior methods that typically
support only single-stage fine-tuning, AutoAdapt provides a
comprehensive framework for full domain adaptation pipelines, including
multi-stage processes such as in-context prompting (eg. RAG), supervised
fine-tuning (SFT), alignment (DPO) and so on. AutoAdapt aims to
*reliably* and *efficiently* generate executable, robust, and
user-aligned *LLM adaptation* plans, overcoming the limitations of
existing AutoML systems.

## Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm

This section details the cumulative regret of AutoRefine algorithm.

#### Setting.

Let $`\Theta`$ be a compact hyperparameter domain equipped with a
continuous–categorical relaxation, and let
$`\widehat{\Theta}\subset\Theta`$ be the finite discretization used by
the acquisition optimizer (e.g., multi-start LBFGS followed by
discretization). Assume the black-box objective
$`f:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}`$ is a sample from a zero-mean Gaussian process
with a squared-exponential (SE/RBF) kernel

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
k_{\text{SE}}(x,x^{\prime})=\sigma_{f}^{2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-x^{\prime}\|^{2}}{2\ell^{2}}\right),
``` |  |

and that observations are noisy:
$`y_{t}=f(\theta_{t})+\varepsilon_{t}`$, where $`\varepsilon_{t}`$ are
$`\sigma`$-sub-Gaussian (independent). The AutoRefine posterior
$`\big(\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}\big)`$ is fit on the dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ that combines ground-truth evaluations
$`\{(\theta_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{t}`$ and LLM-derived trend
pseudo-observations
$`\{(\tilde{\theta}_{j},\tilde{y}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{m_{t}}`$, which are
treated as *unbiased, high-variance* measurements of $`f`$ (conditional
on the GP), i.e.,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{y}_{j}=f(\tilde{\theta}_{j})+\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j},\quad\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}\ \text{is }\tilde{\sigma}\text{-sub-Gaussian with }\tilde{\sigma}\gg\sigma,
``` |  |

and thus incorporated with inflated noise variance so they do not
over-confidently shrink $`\sigma_{t}(\cdot)`$. At round $`t`$,
AutoRefine algorithm selects

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{t}\in\arg\max_{\theta\in\widehat{\Theta}}\;\mu_{t-1}(\theta)+\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\,\sigma_{t-1}(\theta),
``` |  |

with a confidence schedule $`\beta_{t}`$ defined as ([Iwazaki,
2025](#bib.bib17)).

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\beta_{t}=2\ln\left(\frac{2t^{2}\pi^{2}}{3\delta}\right)+2d\ln\left(t^{2}dbr\sqrt{\ln\left(\frac{4da}{\delta}\right)}\right)
``` |  | (1) |

where $`a,b`$ are constants defined in lemma 1 of ([Iwazaki,
2025](#bib.bib17)), $`d`$ is the dimension of the domain and $`r`$ is
the length of the domain. Please refer ([Iwazaki, 2025](#bib.bib17)) for
details. One subtle technical point to note is that in line 19 of
Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.4 AutoRefine ‣ 4 Method ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models"),
the acquisition is done by an LLM that is prompted in-context using the
optimal point from the GP-UCB algorithm. We prompt the LLM to decide
between exploiting the optmized GP-UCB hyperparameters and exploring
novel ones in the search space. As the algorithm progresses, there would
be fewer novel points to explore and the algorithm would rely more on
the GP-UCB optimized point. Thus this acquisition is equivalent to the
epsilon-greedy policy with decay ([Sutton & Barto, 2018](#bib.bib29)),
which asymptotically reduces to the GP-UCB acquisition itself. We need
the LLM sampler as the acquisition as otherwise optimizing the function
manifold may result in the sampler collapsing to the same optimal point
(or one in the vicinity). The LLM sampler acts as a guardrail to prevent
such trivial sampling using its domain knowledge. Let the cumulative
regret be
$`R_{T}:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(f(\theta^{\star})-f(\theta_{t})\big)`$,
where $`\theta^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}f(\theta)`$.

In this part of the proof, we bound the cumulative regret $`R_{T}`$ over
time $`T`$. Here, the time $`T`$ represents the number of iterations
over which the points in the domain (parameter space) are queried to
obtain the function value (results). Note we use an LLM as a surrogate
model to obtain intermediate results and do not perform evaluations by
fitting the network over the sampled parameters and evaluating each
iteration. The complexity of an LLM call is negligible compared to
actually finetuning an LLM over the sampled parameters and evaluating to
obtain the results at that point. As such we only consider the ”actual
function evaluations‘ for the complexity. Define $`F_{a}`$ to be the
augmentation factor i.e. the fraction of the number of data points
queried (by actual function evaluation and LLM surrogate) to the number
of actual model evaluation.

We make use of the below result from ([Srinivas et al.,
2010](#bib.bib28)) (provides bounds on the function value w.r.t. UCB):

###### Lemma C.1 (Confidence bounds ([Srinivas et al., 2010](#bib.bib28))).

With probability $`1-\delta`$ ($`\delta\in(0,1)`$), For any
$`t\in\mathbb{N}_{+}`$, the function value at the queried point
$`x_{t}`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu(x_{t};X_{t-1},y_{t-1})-\beta_{t}^{1/2}\,\sigma(x_{t};X_{t-1})\leq f(x_{t}).
``` |  |

Furthermore, for any $`t\in\mathbb{N}_{+}`$, any function value $`f(x)`$
on $`\mathcal{X}_{t}`$ satisfies

|     |                                                                    |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       f(x)\leq\mu(x;X_{t-1},y_{t-1})+\beta_{t}^{1/2}\,\sigma(x;X_{t-1}).
       ```                                                                 |     |

Using the above result we bound the regret for Autorefine as below:

#### Claim I.

For the SE/RBF kernel, the cumulative regret of the Autorefine algorithm
([1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.4 AutoRefine ‣ 4 Method ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")),
with probability at least $`1-\delta`$ (for any $`\delta\in(0,1)`$) is,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{T_{a}}\;=\;\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{T}{F_{a}}\,\ln^{2}\left(\frac{T}{F_{a}}\right)}\right),
``` |  |

###### Proof.

The proof follows the GP–UCB template ([Iwazaki, 2025](#bib.bib17)) with
two ingredients: (i) high-probability confidence envelopes over the
posterior; and (ii) summability of posterior uncertainties at the points
chosen by UCB.

(1) Confidence Bound: By standard sub-Gaussian concentration and union
bounds on the finite set $`\widehat{\Theta}`$ with the above
$`\beta_{t}`$, we have w.h.p. (probability $`\geq 1-\delta`$) for all
$`t`$ and all $`\theta\in\widehat{\Theta}`$ (c.f. lemma 1 in ([Srinivas
et al., 2010](#bib.bib28)) and
[C.1](#A3.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma C.1 (Confidence bounds ( , )). ‣ Setting. ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f(\theta)-\mu_{t-1}(\theta)\;\leq\;\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\,\sigma_{t-1}(\theta).
``` |  | (2) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f(\theta)-\mu_{t-1}(\theta)\;\geq\;-\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\,\sigma_{t-1}(\theta).
``` |  | (3) |

The inclusion of unbiased pseudo-observations with inflated noise
variance preserves the validity of
 ([2](#A3.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ Proof. ‣ Claim I. ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models"))
and
 ([3](#A3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ Proof. ‣ Claim I. ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")),
as they are treated as additional high-variance measurements; such
points only affect constants in the posterior covariance and thus in
$`\sigma_{t-1}(\cdot)`$.

(2) Instantaneous regret under UCB: Let
$`\Delta_{t}:=f(\theta^{\star})-f(\theta_{t})`$, where $`f`$ is the
actual evaluation (with possible finetuning using the parameters) of the
network using selected parameters and the given data points.

Since the acquisition function ($`\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}f(\theta)`$)
at time $`t`$ selected $`\theta_{t}`$, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mu_{t-1}(\theta_{t})+\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t})`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq\mu_{t-1}(\theta^{\star})+\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta^{\star})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\mu_{t-1}(\theta^{\star})-\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta^{\star})`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\therefore\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t})`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq\mu_{t-1}(\theta^{\star})-\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta^{\star})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\mu_{t-1}(\theta)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\therefore f(\theta^{\star})-\mu_{t-1}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t})`$ |  |
|  |  | , {…From UCB eq. } |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle f(\theta^{\star})-(\mu_{t-1}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle-\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t}))\leq 2\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t})`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle f(\theta^{\star})-f(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t})`$ |  |
|  |  | , {…From LCB eq. } |  |

Thus from above analysis we have

|     |                                                                |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta_{t}\;\leq\;2\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\,\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t}).
       ```                                                             |     | (4) |

(3) Summation and improved SE bound. Since we are only interested in the
regret at every iteration where the function is actually evaluated at
the query point and the GP updated, we discard the iterations with LLM
surrogate queries.
Summing ([4](#A3.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ Proof. ‣ Claim I. ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models"))
over $`t=1,\dots,\frac{T}{F_{a}}`$ gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle R_{T_{a}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\;\leq\;2\sum_{t=1}^{\frac{T}{F_{a}}}\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\,\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t})`$ |  |

For the SE/RBF kernel, a refined analysis of the *realized* input
sequence under UCB shows that the cumulative uncertainty weighted by
$`\sqrt{\beta_{t}}`$ grows as $`\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T\,\ln^{2}T})`$ (c.f.
([Iwazaki, 2025](#bib.bib17))). This yields

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{T_{a}}\;=\;\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{T}{F_{a}}\,\ln^{2}\left(\frac{T}{F_{a}}\right)}\right)
``` |  | (5) |

with high probability.

Effect of pseudo-observations. If we consider the LLM pseudo
observations in the regret, the bound comes out to be the following
(same as in ([Iwazaki, 2025](#bib.bib17)))

|     |                                                    |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{T}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{T\,\ln^{2}T}\right)
       ```                                                 |     | (6) |

Because pseudo-observations are incorporated as unbiased high-variance
points, they do not invalidate
 ([3](#A3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ Proof. ‣ Claim I. ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")),
 ([2](#A3.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ Proof. ‣ Claim I. ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models"));
they only alter constants in the posterior computation and hence in the
final constant multiplying $`\sqrt{T\,\ln^{2}T}`$. Therefore the rate is
unchanged, concluding the proof of Part I bounding the regret from
above. ∎

For the part II on the lower bound for the number of iterations,
consider the *simple regret* after $`T`$ rounds to be

|     |                                                             |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{T}:=f(\theta^{\star})-\max_{1\leq t\leq T}f(\theta_{t}),
       ```                                                          |     |

where $`\theta^{\star}`$ is the global maximiser of $`f`$. From equation
[6](#A3.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ Proof. ‣ Claim I. ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Bounds on the Autorefine algorithm ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
we obtain the average simple regret (over $`T`$ iterations) as

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{T}=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\Bigg(\sqrt{\frac{\ln^{2}T}{T}}\Bigg).
       ```                                                                |     |

#### Claim II.

To guarantee $`r_{T}\leq\varepsilon`$ for some $`\varepsilon>0`$, the
number of actual function evaluation iterations $`T_{a}`$ must satisfy

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T_{a}=\Omega\!\Bigg(\frac{\ln^{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{F_{a}\varepsilon^{2}}\Bigg).
``` |  |

###### Proof.

From the regret rate,

|     |                                      |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{T}\leq c\sqrt{\frac{\ln^{2}T}{T}}
       ```                                   |     |

for some constant $`c>0`$. To enforce $`r_{T}\leq\varepsilon`$, we
require

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c\sqrt{\frac{\ln^{2}T}{T}}\leq\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sqrt{\frac{\ln^{2}T}{T}}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{c}.
``` |  |

Squaring both sides gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\ln^{2}T}{T}\leq\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{c^{2}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\geq\frac{c^{2}\ln^{2}T}{\varepsilon^{2}}.
``` |  |

This is an implicit inequality because $`T`$ appears inside
$`\ln^{2}T`$. For large $`T`$, $`\ln T`$ grows slowly compared to $`T`$,
so we approximate $`\ln T\approx\ln(1/\varepsilon)`$ (since $`T`$ will
scale like $`1/\varepsilon^{2}`$ in lower bound). Substituting yields

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle T`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Omega\!\Bigg(\frac{\ln^{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\Bigg)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle F_{a}T_{a}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Omega\!\Bigg(\frac{\ln^{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\Bigg)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle T_{a}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Omega\!\Bigg(\frac{\ln^{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{F_{a}\varepsilon^{2}}\Bigg)`$ |  |

which establishes the lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. ∎

###### Remark C.2 (On LLM guidance and constants).

If trend points are slightly misspecified with bounded bias
$`b(\theta)`$ but are re-centered (or modeled with hyperparameters that
absorb the bias), the confidence envelopes remain valid up to a constant
slack, which is absorbed into the choice of $`\beta_{t}`$; the
asymptotic $`\sqrt{T\,\ln^{2}T}`$ rate is preserved while constants
improve when LLM guidance focuses the search in informative regions. If
a fixed bias $`B>0`$ were injected without correction, an additional
linear term $`\mathcal{O}(BT)`$ would appear from
$`\Delta_{t}\leq 2\sqrt{\beta_{t}}\sigma_{t-1}(\theta_{t})+2B`$; thus,
bias calibration or high-variance downweighting is essential to maintain
sublinear regret.

###### Remark C.3 (On iteration complexity).

The iteration complexity grows quadratically with $`1/\varepsilon`$ and
only polylogarithmically with the domain size (via
$`\ln^{2}(1/\varepsilon)`$). For example, to achieve
$`\varepsilon=0.05`$ (for e.g. within 5% of the optimal accuracy) with
augmentation factor $`F_{a}=100`$, we need

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle T_{\min}`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\ln^{2}(20)}{100\times(0.05)^{2}}\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\approx\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{(3)^{2}}{0.25}\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\approx\mathcal{O}\left(10\right)\text{ iterations.}`$ |  |

Note, our algorithm does not change the asymptotic complexity compared
to the GP-UCB algorithm but only changes the constant factors in the
complexity. However, the gains are practically significant as our
algorithm only needs few tens of iterations vs perhaps thousands to
converge to the optimal point, which is desirable considering the costly
training of LLMs.

## Appendix D Adaptation Configuration Graph

In this section, we describe in detail the design of the ACG utilized to
run the multi agent planning pipeline. Figure
[8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix D Adaptation Configuration Graph ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
illustrates the Adaptation Configuration Graph (ACG) used in our
framework to structure and constrain the space of large language model
(LLM) domain adaptation workflows. The ACG is a directed acyclic graph
that explicitly encodes high‑level adaptation strategies, their
dependencies, and the corresponding parameterized training
configurations, enabling systematic and reliable planning of multi‑stage
adaptation pipelines.

At the highest level, the ACG branches from a root adapt node into
alternative adaptation strategies, including retrieval‑augmented
generation (RAG), supervised fine‑tuning (SFT), and preference‑based
alignment (DPO). Each strategy node captures a semantically distinct
mode of adaptation and is connected via requires edges to the concrete
configuration blocks needed to instantiate that strategy. This design
allows the planner to reason explicitly over which adaptation techniques
are applicable under given data, resource, and user constraints, rather
than treating the pipeline as an unstructured sequence of
hyperparameters.

For RAG, the graph specifies the required retrieval configuration,
including the embedding model, retriever parameters (e.g., top‑k), and
the base model used for generation. This separation allows
retrieval‑specific choices to be optimized independently of downstream
training decisions. For SFT and DPO, the ACG links the corresponding
strategy nodes to detailed training configurations that define the base
model, optimization hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, gradient
accumulation), logging and evaluation intervals, and training duration.
By explicitly modeling these configurations as graph nodes, the ACG
exposes the hierarchical structure of LLM adaptation decisions.

The graph further captures parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning (PEFT) as an
intermediate abstraction. Both SFT and DPO may route through a PEFT
node, which in turn branches into concrete techniques such as LoRA and
prefix tuning. Each PEFT variant is associated with its own parameter
block, specifying method‑specific hyperparameters (e.g., LoRA rank and
scaling factors, prefix length) as well as shared efficiency settings
such as quantization type. This explicit factoring enables the planner
to reuse shared structure while still exploring method‑specific
configurations.

Overall, the ACG serves two key purposes. First, it narrows the
effective search space by enforcing valid structural dependencies
between adaptation stages and parameters, thereby preventing ill‑formed
or non‑executable pipelines. Second, it provides a transparent and
interpretable representation of the adaptation workflow, which can be
traversed and refined by downstream optimization components. By
grounding pipeline construction in the ACG, our framework achieves
reliable execution while retaining flexibility to support diverse
adaptation strategies and training regimes.

![Refer to caption](2603.08181v1/figures/acg_detailed.png)

Figure 8: Adaptation Configuration Graph (ACG) for the LLM adaptation
pipeline with example parameter values at each parameter node.

## Appendix E Multi Agent System

In this section we detail the agents used in the multi-agent pipeline
and the corresponding prompts. All agents use OpenAI’s GPT-4.1-mini as
the underlying model. Below are the agents used in the system:

### E.1 Proposal Agents

Best Practice Agent consolidates empirical insights from prior training
pipelines, model cards, and benchmark results. It provides principled
priors over adaptation strategies, hyperparameter ranges, and
architectural choices, enabling the system to initialize planning in a
region of the configuration space that historically yields strong
performance.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Research Agent processed the literature, technical reports, and model
documentation (for eg. gathered by the retrieval agent) to identify
emerging techniques or underexplored alternatives. This ensures that the
system incorporates innovations beyond those reflected in curated
best‑practice corpora.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Knowledge Retriever Agent dynamically retrieves and aggregates knowledge
from multiple web sources (arXiv papers, Hugging Face model/data cards,
and web search relevant to a user’s task. It queries these sources, then
summarizes the collected information into actionable insights using an
LLM. This agent helps provide up-to-date, real-world context about
state-of-the-art models, techniques, and best practices to support
downstream decision-making in the multi-agent framework.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.2 Critic Agents

User Preference Agent encodes user‑specified constraints such as compute
budgets, training preferences, method restrictions, and domain‑specific
requirements and enforces them throughout the adaptation process. It
operationalizes user intent by filtering infeasible configurations and
steering the system toward personalized solutions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Data Agent analyzes the statistics of the provided dataset, including
size, token distributions, domain characteristics, entropy measures,
label properties etc. It transforms these signals into actionable
quantitative summaries of the dataset. This agent also critiques the
proposal based on data constraints.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.3 Aggregator Agent

Aggregator Agent integrates outputs from all upstream agents into a
unified context representation. It resolves conflicts, normalizes
heterogeneous signals, and constructs the information state consumed by
the multi‑agent planner. This aggregation step ensures coherent and
consistent decision‑making across the system.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix F Datasets

We conduct experiments on diverse domains to demonstrate the
generalizability of *AutoAdapt*. The domains are as follows: 1)
Mathematical Reasoning 2) Medical Question Answering 3) Legal 4) Root
Cause Analysis of Cloud Incidents (Proprietary Dataset) 5) Natural
Language 6) Ecommerce 7) Programming 8) Generic reasoning

Specifically we select the following benchmark and real world datasets:

\(1\) MATH ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib14)) dataset by UC Berkeley
focused on mathematical reasoning, covering algebra, calculus, and
advanced problem-solving.

\(2\) MedQA ([Jin et al., 2020](#bib.bib18)) is a medical question
answering dataset requiring domain-specific knowledge and reasoning.

\(3\) CaseHold ([Zheng et al., 2021](#bib.bib37)) is a legal reasoning
dataset for predicting case outcomes, testing adaptation to specialized
legal language

\(4\) PEM is a customer dataset containing pre-engineering level math
questions and answers.

\(5\) RCA is a proprietary dataset containing the root cause analysis of
cloud incidents in a large scale cloud service provider.

\(6\) ARC ([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib6)) consists of multiple-choice
science questions spanning elementary to middle-school curricula,
designed to assess commonsense reasoning and knowledge integration
across diverse scientific domains.

\(7\) MBPP ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib2)) is a code generation
benchmark composed of python problems

\(8\) Ecomm ([Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) is a task of
classification of e-commerce products into relevant categories.

\(9\) Entail ([Trirat et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) is a task of natural
language inference given premise and hypothesis.

\(10\) When2Call ([Ross et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)) is designed to deduce
tool invocation ability.

## Appendix G Best-Practices Knowledge Base

In this section we explain the construction of the best practices KB and
provide studies on the best practices retrieved and the consistency and
relevance of the recommendations provided using these.

### G.1 KB Construction

To ground the adaptation planning process in empirical evidence and
widely adopted practices, we construct a Best‑Practices Knowledge Base
(KB) that aggregates and structures information from diverse public
sources on large language model (LLM) training, adaptation, and
evaluation. The primary goal of the KB is to expose reliable priors over
model choices, adaptation strategies, and hyperparameter configurations,
which can be leveraged by the multi‑agent planner to generate executable
and effective adaptation pipelines.

Knowledge Sources We curate the KB from multiple complementary sources
that reflect both community standards and state‑of‑the‑art empirical
results. Specifically, we collect information offline from: (i) model
cards and dataset cards hosted on Hugging Face, which provide structured
descriptions of training regimes, datasets, parameter choices,
evaluation metrics, and reported performance; (ii) fine‑tuning code
repositories and notebooks from platforms such as GitHub and Unsloth,
which expose concrete implementation details and hyperparameter settings
used in practice; and (iii) leaderboards and evaluation summaries from
Papers with Code, which link datasets to top‑performing models and
report comparative metrics. These sources provide complementary
perspectives, ranging from high‑level summaries to low‑level
configuration details.

Knowledge Extraction and Structuring Raw information from the above
sources is heterogeneous and largely unstructured. To address this, we
employ an LLM‑based extraction pipeline to convert documents and code
into structured representations. For each model or dataset entry, we
extract salient attributes such as dataset domain, size, task type,
input–output characteristics, model family, parameter count, training
pipeline (e.g., SFT, PEFT, DPO), and reported hyperparameter ranges. In
the case of code repositories, we further extract explicit parameter
instantiations (e.g., learning rate, batch size, number of epochs,
PEFT‑specific settings) from training scripts and notebooks. All
extracted items are normalized and stored as structured records. We
manually validate a handful of the extracted data, however due to the
scale of the data manual verification of the entire KB is left to future
works.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Indexing and Retrieval Each record in the KB is indexed using a
combination of semantic descriptors (task type, domain, dataset
characteristics) and model attributes (architecture family, training
method, parameter scale). At planning time, the user task description
and dataset metadata are used to query the KB and retrieve a set of
relevant model–dataset–configuration tuples. This retrieval step
provides the multi‑agent system with concrete empirical precedents drawn
from similar tasks and domains, serving as an evidence‑based starting
point for decision making.

Leveraging Best Practices for Adaptation Planning The KB is directly
consumed by the Best‑Practice Agent during the planning stage. Given a
candidate adaptation decision (e.g., selecting PEFT over full
fine‑tuning), the agent uses retrieved KB entries to justify choices and
to propose bounded hyperparameter ranges rather than arbitrary or overly
broad search spaces. For example, learning rate ranges, batch size
options, or training epoch counts are derived from configurations that
have been demonstrated to work on comparable tasks and model scales.
These KB‑derived ranges are subsequently refined during the AutoRefine
stage based on user data and observed performance. Figure shows the
retrieval schema by best practice agent from the KB.

![Refer to
caption](2603.08181v1/figures/autoadapt_bestpractice_retrieval.png)

Figure 9: Best practices retrieval pipeline from KB.

Scope and Limitations The KB is not intended to be exhaustive. Instead,
it functions as a practical, curated prior over adaptation decisions for
the domains and tasks considered in our experiments. We additionally
support dynamic, query‑time retrieval to incorporate recent or
task‑specific information beyond the offline corpus when needed. This
design strikes a balance between coverage, accuracy, and computational
efficiency. Overall, the Best‑Practices Knowledge Base enables
*AutoAdapt* to ground its recommendations in established empirical
evidence in LLM adaptation, reducing reliance on ad‑hoc heuristics or
unconstrained exploration, while maintaining flexibility to adapt to
user‑specific data and requirements.

### G.2 Dispersion Index of Recommended Parameter Ranges

To quantify the diversity of hyperparameter range recommendations
produced by our multi-agent framework, we introduce the Dispersion Index
(DI). The DI captures the degree of variability across a set of
configurations by jointly considering categorical and numeric
dimensions. Unlike pairwise similarity measures that focus on individual
comparisons, our metric summarizes the overall spread of the
recommendation set, providing a single interpretable score.

Formally, let $`\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{N}\}`$ denote the set
of recommended configurations. Each configuration comprises categorical
parameters (e.g., activation functions, optimizer choices) and numeric
parameters (e.g., learning rate, batch size). For any pair
$`(c_{i},c_{j})`$, we compute:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Sim}(c_{i},c_{j})=\alpha\cdot J(c_{i},c_{j})+(1-\alpha)\cdot\overline{\text{IoU}}(c_{i},c_{j}),
``` |  | (7) |

where $`J(\cdot,\cdot)`$ is the Jaccard similarity over categorical
tokens, $`\overline{\text{IoU}}(\cdot,\cdot)`$ is the weighted average
Intersection-over-Union across numeric ranges, and $`\alpha\in[0,1]`$
balances the contributions of categorical and numeric components. The
Dispersion Index is then defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{DI}=\frac{2}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i<j}\big(1-\text{Sim}(c_{i},c_{j})\big).
``` |  | (8) |

Intuitively, DI approaches zero when all configurations are nearly
identical and increases as recommendations become more diverse. By
incorporating both discrete and continuous dimensions, DI provides a
holistic measure of variability that is particularly suited for
mixed-type hyperparameter spaces. This metric enables us to assess
whether the optimizer explores the search space broadly or converges to
a narrow region, which is critical for evaluating
exploration–exploitation trade-offs in automated tuning.

![Refer to caption](2603.08181v1/figures/dispersion_boxplot.png)

(a) Dispersion index by dataset.

![Refer to caption](2603.08181v1/figures/relevance_boxplot.png)

(b) Relevance scores by dataset.

Figure 10: (Left) Boxplot showing the dispersion index metric for each
dataset. We observe a median score around $`0.5`$, indicating a balance
between consistency and diversity in the recommendations. (Right)
Boxplot showing relevance scores of the retrieved best practices. We
observe consistently high relevance across datasets.

Figure [10(a)](#A7.F10.sf1 "Figure 10(a) ‣ Figure 10 ‣ G.2 Dispersion Index of Recommended Parameter Ranges ‣ Appendix G Best-Practices Knowledge Base ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
reports the distribution of dissimilarity scores across three datasets:
PEM, RCA, and MedQA. We observe that the median dispersion for PEM and
RCA lies around 0.45, while MedQA exhibits a higher median near 0.55
with a broader inter-quartile range. Overall, the dispersion values
cluster around 0.5, indicating a balance between consistency and
variability in the recommended hyperparameter configurations. This
suggests that our optimization strategy avoids excessive convergence to
a single configuration while maintaining sufficient overlap to ensure
stability. Notably, MedQA shows greater variability, reflecting the
increased complexity and heterogeneity of this task, whereas PEM and RCA
remain comparatively more consistent.

### G.3 Recommendation Relevance

In order to study the relevance of the best practice sources used for
recommendations, we perform a human annotation. Specifically we employ
two human experts to review the best practice sources retrieved as well
as the task and final recommendations. The annotators then score each
retrieved source in a binary manner i.e. 0 if it is not relevant to the
task and 1 if it is relevant. We then average these scores across all
sources for a given task and run. We experiment on the three datasets:
PEM, RCA, MedQA and run the best practice agent 10 times per dataset.
The results are reported in figure
[10(b)](#A7.F10.sf2 "Figure 10(b) ‣ Figure 10 ‣ G.2 Dispersion Index of Recommended Parameter Ranges ‣ Appendix G Best-Practices Knowledge Base ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models"),
where we see a high relevance across all datasets confirming that the
retrieved sources are indeed relevant to the task. In order to eliminate
the human bias, we compute the Cohen’s Kappa score (([Cohen et al.,
2007](#bib.bib7))) and find a high inter rater agreement ( $`>0.9`$)
between the annotators.

### G.4 Example Recommendations

Figure
 [11](#A7.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ G.5 Example Best Practice Retrievals ‣ Appendix G Best-Practices Knowledge Base ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")
summarizes an example hyperparameter range recommended by our
multi-agent pipeline for the MedQA dataset. The configuration includes
both categorical and numeric range parameters, reflecting flexibility in
batch size, accumulation steps, and learning rate, while maintaining
structural flags such as gradient checkpointing.

The proposed hyperparameter search space is designed to achieve an
optimal balance between computational efficiency and model performance.
By constraining the search to a compact yet expressive set of
configurations, we enable systematic exploration while mitigating the
risk of combinatorial explosion.

Model Selection. Fixing the backbone to meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
ensures architectural consistency and leverages a strong
instruction-tuned foundation, thereby reducing variance attributable to
model choice.

Categorical Parameters. The discrete sets for
per_device_train_batch_size ({2, 4, 8, 12}) and
gradient_accumulation_steps ({4, 8, 16}) provide flexibility in
effective batch size scaling. These choices are informed by practical
hardware constraints, ensuring that each candidate configuration is
feasible for typical GPU memory budgets.

Continuous Parameters. The learning rate interval
$`[10^{-5},5\times 10^{-4}]`$ captures the regime most relevant for
fine-tuning large language models: sufficiently small to prevent
catastrophic forgetting yet broad enough to accommodate task-specific
convergence behaviour. Similarly, the epoch range of $`[3,10]`$ offers
adaptability across datasets of varying complexity while avoiding
overfitting.

Efficiency and Robustness. By prioritising high-impact parameters and
fixing structural flags such as gradient_checkpointing, the search space
remains tractable without sacrificing diversity. This design accelerates
convergence, reduces computational overhead, and supports
reproducibility across heterogeneous tasks.

In summary, the recommended parameter ranges exemplify an efficient
search space that balances exploration and exploitation, enabling robust
performance gains under realistic resource constraints.

### G.5 Example Best Practice Retrievals

To ensure robust and efficient fine-tuning of large language models for
medical question answering (MedQA), we consolidated a set of
authoritative resources from Hugging Face and related repositories.
These resources provide guidance on model configuration,
parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), and domain-specific adaptation
strategies.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Relevance for MedQA Task. These resources collectively address the
critical aspects of domain adaptation for medical question answering.
The Llama 3 configuration and Hugging Face finetuning guides provide
foundational instructions for model initialization and training
workflows. PEFT and LoRA-based methods enable parameter-efficient
adaptation, reducing memory footprint while preserving performance.
QLoRA introduces quantization-aware optimization, further improving
efficiency without compromising accuracy. Domain-specific insights from
the Medical LLMs overview and curated medical QA datasets ensure that
the fine-tuned models capture clinical reasoning patterns and
terminology. Note we ensure that the target dataset link is not present
in the retrieved resources to prevent data leakage. Together, these best
practices form a comprehensive toolkit for achieving high-quality,
resource-efficient adaptation in downstream applications.

## Appendix H Experimental Setup

In this section, we highlight the detailed experimental setup and
justify its completeness in proving the efficiency of *AutoAdapt* over
existing LLM-based AutoML based methods. To make the comparison fair
across all baselines, all agents are implemented using the same model as
AutoAdapt (i.e OpenAI’s GPT-4.1-mini). In order to prevent data leakage,
we remove entries of the exact benchmark dataset being evaluated, if
present in KB. More concretely, experiments are conducted within the
following two setups:

- •
  Template Free (TF) Setting: Within this setup, we evaluate each
  method’s proficiency at generating an end-to-end pipeline under no
  explicit constraints, except for a simple prompt describing user
  requirements with respect to domain, accuracy and inference speed -
  mimcing the requirements of a user with no domain knowledge of LLMs.
  This gives the candidates full autonomy over the choice of model,
  adaptation technique and parameters. The prompt is kept consistent
  across all baselines. However, despite a 100% success rate
  demonstrated by *AutoAdapt*, other methods fail to produce final code
  templates that execute without any errors. To quantify the ability of
  the baselines to produce executable code, we manually fix errors in
  the code templates produced by baseline methods, and report the
  Success Rate of each method as:
  $`\text{Success Rate (SR)}=\frac{1}{1+\text{number of iterations}}`$.
  The prompt format is as follows:

  ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
- •
  Template Aware (TA) Setting: This setup is meant to offer a fairer
  comparison between the baselines. In this setup, we augment the other
  baselines with the following AutoAdapt resources - (a) Adaptation
  Configuration Graph (ACG), (b) best practices knowledge base (KB),
  and (c) respective templates for SFT, DPO and RAG. This ensures a
  default success rate of 100% and judges the baselines purely on their
  ability to make an informed decision regarding the parameter choices.
  Since performance on Natural Language benchmarks is highly contingent
  on the base model and duration of training, we fix the model across a
  task along with the number of epochs set to 1. The prompt format is as
  follows:

  ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We utilize the proposed method for each dataset to evaluate the trained
models. However, for datasets that lack a well-defined method of
evaluation, we adopt an LLM-based equivalence matching with the correct
labels to evaluate the models. The evaluation method and metric for each
dataset is summarized in the following table, followed by the prompt
formats:

| Dataset | Method of Evaluation | Metric |
|----|----|----|
| UC Berkeley MATH | [OpenAI/simple_evals](https://github.com/openai/simple-evals) | Accuracy |
| MedQA | LLM-based equivalence matching (P1) | Accuracy |
| CaseHold | LLM-based equivalence matching (P1) | Accuracy |
| PEM | LLM-based answer extraction (P3) + equivalence matching (P1) | Accuracy |
| RCA | LLM-as-a-Judge (P2) | Average Score |
| ARC | LLM-based equivalence matching (P1) | Accuracy |
| MBPP+ | Evalplus ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib22)) | Accuracy |
| When2Call | LLM-based equivalence matching (P1) | Accuracy |
| E-commerce | Direct Comparison | Accuracy |
| Textual Entailment | Direct Comparison | Accuracy |

We further normalize the accuracies and average scores from 0 to 1, and
report it as NPS (Normalized Performance Scores). We report the
Cumulative Score defined as:
$`\text{Cumulative Score}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\text{NPS}+\text{SR})`$. The
detailed results used to construct the radar plots in
[Figure 4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ AutoAdapt: An Automated Domain Adaptation Framework for Large Language Models")

## Appendix K Success Rate Analysis

In this section, we provide a sample of manual iterations performed to
fix the code templates outputted for the MedQA dataset by the baselines,
for transparency. Note, success rate (SR) defined as
$`SR=\frac{1}{1+\texttt{number of iterations}}`$ depends on the number
of iterations required to obtain a runnable pipeline and is intended to
capture engineering reliability, not model quality. Without these
corrective steps the baseline models completely fail to execute and the
raw success rate would be 0% for all baselines.
````
